#Text=The loss on soaking in cold water, unless the water is preserved, is seen

#Text=Potatoes are rich in important potash salts; by
#Text= boiling a large quantity is lost, by steaming less and by baking in the
#Text= skins, scarcely any.
#Text=The flavour is also much better after baking.
#Text=The usual addition of common salt (sodium-chloride) to boiled potatoes is
#Text=no proper substitute for the loss of their natural saline constituents.
#Text=Natural and properly cooked foods are so rich in sodium chloride and other
#Text= salts that the addition of common salt is unnecessary.
#Text=An excess of the
#Text= latter excites thirst and spoils the natural flavour of the food.
#Text=It is
#Text= the custom, especially in restaurants, to add a large quantity of salt to
#Text= pulse, savoury food, potatoes and soups.
#Text=Bakers  '   brown bread is usually
#Text= very salt, and sometimes white is also.
#Text=In some persons much salt causes
#Text= irritation of the skin, and the writer has knowledge of the salt food of
#Text= vegetarian restaurants causing or increasing dandruff.
#Text=As a rule, fondness
#Text= for salt is an acquired taste, and after its discontinuance for a time,
#Text= food thus flavoured becomes unpalatable.
#Text=Organic Compounds are formed by living organisms (a few can also be
#Text= produced by chemical means).
#Text=They are entirely decomposed by combustion.
#Text=The Non-Nitrogenous Organic Compounds are commonly called carbon
#Text= compounds or heat-producers, but these terms are also descriptive of the
#Text= nitrogenous compounds.
#Text=These contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only, and
#Text= furnish by their oxidation or combustion in the body the necessary heat,
#Text= muscular and nervous energy.
#Text=The final product of their combustion is
#Text=containing none.
#Text=A moderate quantity favours digestion and the bodily
#Text= health.
#Text=In cold weather more should be taken.
#Text=In the Arctic regions the
#Text= Esquimaux consume enormous quantities.
#Text=Nuts are generally rich in oil.
#Text=Oatmeal contains more than any of the other cereals (27 analyses gave from
#Text= 8 to 12.3 per cent.)
#Text=The most esteemed and dearest oil is Almond.
#Text=What is called Peach-kernel
#Text= oil (Oleum Amygdalæ Persicæ), but which in commerce includes the oil
#Text= obtained from plum and apricot stones, is almost as tasteless and useful,
#Text= whilst it is considerably cheaper.
#Text=It is a very agreeable and useful food.
#Text=It is often added to, as an adulterant, or substituted for the true Almond
#Text= oil.
#Text=The best qualities of Olive oil are much esteemed, though they are
#Text= not as agreeable to English taste as the oil previously mentioned.
#Text=The
#Text= best qualities are termed Virgin, Extra Sublime and Sublime.
#Text=Any that has
#Text= been exposed for more than a short time to the light and heat of a shop
#Text= window should be rejected, as the flavour is affected.
#Text=It should be kept
#Text= in a cool place.
#Text=Not only does it vary much in freedom from acid and
#Text= rancidity, but is frequently adulterated.
#Text=Two other cheaper oils deserve
#Text= mention.
#Text=The "cold-drawn" Arachis oil (pea-nut or earth-nut oil) has a
#Text= pleasant flavour, resembling that of kidney beans.
#Text=The "cold-drawn" Sesamé
#Text=oil has an agreeable taste, and is considered equal to Olive oil for
#Text= edible purposes.
#Text=The best qualities are rather difficult to obtain; those
#Text= usually sold being much inferior to Peach-kernel and Olive oils.
#Text=Cotton-seed oil is the cheapest of the edible ones.
#Text=Salad oil, not sold
#Text= under any descriptive name, is usually refined Cotton-seed oil, with
#Text= perhaps a little Olive oil to impart a richer flavour.
#Text=The solid fats sold as butter and lard substitutes, consist of deodorised
#Text= cocoanut oil, and they are excellent for cooking purposes.
#Text=It is claimed
#Text= that biscuits, &c., made from them may be kept for a much longer period,
#Text= without showing any trace of rancidity, than if butter or lard had been
#Text= used.
#Text=They are also to be had agreeably flavoured by admixture with
#Text= almond, walnut, &c., "cream."
#Text=The better quality oils are quite as wholesome as the best fresh butter,
#Text= and better than most butter as sold.
#Text=Bread can be dipped into the oil, or
#Text= a little solid vegetable fat spread on it.
#Text=The author prefers to pour a
#Text= little Peach-kernel oil upon some ground walnut kernels (or other ground
#Text= nuts in themselves rich in oil), mix with a knife to a suitable
#Text= consistency and spread upon the bread.
#Text=Pine-kernels are very oily, and can
#Text=be used in pastry in the place of butter or lard.
#Text=Whenever oils are mentioned, without a prefix, the fixed or fatty oils are
#Text= always understood.
#Text=The volatile or essential oils are a distinct class.
#Text=Occasionally, the fixed oils are called hydrocarbons, but hydrocarbon
#Text= oils are quite different and consist of carbon and hydrogen alone.
#Text=Of
#Text= these, petroleum is incapable of digestion, whilst others are poisonous.
#Text=Vegetable Acids are composed of the same three elements and undergo
#Text= combustion into the same compounds as the carbohydrates.
#Text=They rouse the
#Text= appetite, stimulate digestion, and finally form carbonates in combination
#Text= with the alkalies, thus increasing the alkalinity of the blood.
#Text=The chief
#Text= vegetable acids are: malic acid, in the apple, pear, cherry, &c.; citric
#Text= acid, in the lemon, lime, orange, gooseberry, cranberry, strawberry,
#Text= raspberry, &c.; tartaric acid, in the grape, pineapple, &c.
#Text=Some place these under Class III. or food adjuncts.
#Text=Oxalic acid (except
#Text= when in the insoluble state of calcium oxalate), and several other acids
#Text= are poisonous.

#Text=Cookery.
#Text=--Flesh is easier to digest raw.
#Text=A few, on the advice of their
#Text= doctors, eat minced raw flesh, raw beef juice and even fresh warm blood.
#Text=Such practice is abhorrent to every person of refinement.
#Text=Cooking lessens
#Text= the offensive appearance and qualities of flesh and changes the flavour;
#Text=thorough cooking also destroys any parasites that may be present.
#Text=Raw
#Text= flesh is more stimulating to the animal passions, and excites ferocity in
#Text= both man and animals.
#Text=If the old argument was valid, that as flesh is much
#Text= nearer in composition and quality to our own flesh and tissues, it is
#Text= therefore our best food, we do wrong in coagulating the albuminoids,
#Text= hardening the muscle substance and scorching it by cooking.
#Text=Fruits when ripe and in good condition are best eaten raw; cooking spoils
#Text= the flavour.
#Text=Food requiring mastication and encouraging insalivation is
#Text= the best.
#Text=Food is frequently made too sloppy or liquid, and is eaten too
#Text= hot, thus favouring indigestion and decay of the teeth.
#Text=The cereals and
#Text= pulses can only with difficulty be eaten raw.
#Text=When cooked in water the
#Text= starch granules swell and break up, the plant cells are ruptured, the
#Text= fibres are separated and the nutritious matter rendered easy of digestion.
#Text=The flavour is greatly improved.
#Text=Cooking increases our range and variety
#Text= of food.
#Text=The civilised races use it to excess and over-season their
#Text= dishes, favouring over-eating.
#Text=If baking powders are used they should only be of the best makes.
#Text=They
#Text= should be composed of sodium bicarbonate and tartaric acid, in such
#Text=much pleasanter, more satisfying, and better flavoured than white; indeed,
#Text= the latter is described as insipid.
#Text=Most bakers  '   bread is of
#Text= unsatisfactory quality.
#Text=Flour and bread contain very little fat, the
#Text= absence of which is considered a defect.
#Text=This is remedied by the addition
#Text= of butter, fat or oil, or by nuts, &c., which are rich in oil.
#Text=These may
#Text= be mixed with the flour prior to cooking, or used afterwards.
#Text=Oats contain a substance called avenin, apparently an alkaloid, which has
#Text= an irritating action; the quantity is variable.
#Text=It is to this that the
#Text= so-called heating effect of oatmeal on some persons is due.
#Text=Prepared Cereals or Breakfast Foods.
#Text=--Analyses were made of 34 of these
#Text= cereal preparations by Weems and Ellis (Iowa State College Agricultural
#Text= Bulletin, 1904).
#Text=They report that the foods possess no nutritive value in
#Text= excess of ordinary food materials; that the claim made for many
#Text= pre-digested foods are valueless, and no reliance can be placed on the
#Text= statement that they are remedies for any disease.
#Text=Oatmeal and other cereals are sold in packets as being partially cooked.
#Text=We do not doubt that they have been subjected to a dry heat, but this has
#Text=scarcely any effect on their starch and other constituents.
#Text=The difference
#Text= is a mechanical one.
#Text=In rolled oats the grains are so cracked and broken,
#Text= that on boiling with water, the water readily penetrates and more quickly
#Text= cooks them throughout.
#Text=There are other prepared cereal foods, but we doubt
#Text= whether they are thoroughly cooked after the short boiling directed on the
#Text= labels.
#Text=They are a great convenience where it is difficult to get the time
#Text= necessary for cooking the ordinary cereals.
#Text=Coarsely ground wheat is too
#Text= irritating when made into porridge, but there are some granulated wheats
#Text= sold in packets, which are quite suitable.
#Text=The Ralston breakfast food is
#Text= excellent.
#Text=They are rich in the phosphates and salts, found in the outer
#Text= part of the grain.
#Text=One cereal preparation called Grape Nuts, has had its
#Text= starch converted into maltose and dextrin (maltose being a sugar), by a
#Text= scientific application of the diastase of the grain.
#Text=It is consequently
#Text= easier of digestion and requires no cooking.
#Text=It is beneficial for some
#Text= forms of indigestion.
#Text=There are several competing foods of less merit, the
#Text= starch being less perfectly changed; one at least of which is
#Text= objectionably salt.
#Text=Properly cooked starch is readily digested by healthy
#Text= persons, and for them malted food is of no special value.
#Text=Pulse, or Legumes, includes haricots and other beans, peas and lentils.
#Text=The proteid contained is that variety known as legumin, which is either
#Text= the same, or is closely allied, to the casein of milk and cheese.
#Text=Pulse is
#Text= very rich in proteid, the dried kinds in general use, contain 24 or 25 per
#Text= cent.
#Text=The richest is the soy-bean, which is used in China and Japan, it
#Text= contains 35 per cent., besides 19 per cent. of fat.
#Text=Pulse requires
#Text= thorough cooking, haricots taking the longest time.
#Text=Split lentils are
#Text= cooked sooner, and are better digested; this is chiefly due to the removal
#Text= of the skins.
#Text=The haricots, bought from small grocers who have a slow
#Text= sale, are often old, and will not cook tender.
#Text=Pulse is best adapted to
#Text= the labouring classes; the sedentary should eat it sparingly, it is liable
#Text= to cause flatulence or accumulation of gas in the intestines, and
#Text= constipation.
#Text=Haricots are easier to digest when mashed and mixed with
#Text= other food.
#Text=Pulse was formerly stated to leave much undigested residue.
#Text=Recent experiments have shown that it is satisfactorily digested under
#Text= favourable conditions.
#Text=Strümpell found beans in their skins to leave a
#Text= large proportion of proteid matter unabsorbed.
#Text=Lentil meal mixed with
#Text= other food was digested in a perfectly satisfactory manner.
#Text=Another
#Text= experimenter (Rubner) found that when even the very large quantity of
#Text= 1-1/8 pound of dried split peas per day were eaten, only 17 per cent. of
#Text= proteid matter was unabsorbed, which compares very well with the 11 per
#Text=cent. of proteid left from a macaroni diet, with which the same man was
#Text= fed at another time.
#Text=Had a reasonable quantity of peas been eaten per day,
#Text= the quantity undigested would probably have differed little from that of
#Text= other foods.
#Text=Nuts are, as a rule, very rich in oil and contain a fair proportion of
#Text= proteid; when well masticated they are a very valuable food.
#Text=Walnuts are
#Text= one of the best, and the kernels can be purchased shelled, thus avoiding
#Text= much trouble.
#Text=They can be finely ground in a nut-mill and used for several
#Text= purposes, mixed in the proportion of about two ounces to the pound of
#Text= wheatmeal they produce a rich flavoured bread.
#Text=They can also he used in
#Text= sweet cakes and in rich puddings to increase their food value, lightness
#Text= and taste.
#Text=Pine kernels being very oily, can be used with flour in the
#Text= place of lard or butter.
#Text=Fruits are generally looked upon as luxuries, rather than as food
#Text= capable of supplying a meal or a substantial part of one.
#Text=They are usually
#Text= eaten only when the appetite has been appeased by what is considered more
#Text= substantial fare.
#Text=Fresh fruits contain a larger proportion of water than
#Text= nearly all other raw foods, and consequently the proportion of
#Text=nourishment is small; but we must not despise them on this account.
#Text=Milk
#Text= contains as much or more water.
#Text=Certain foods which in the raw state
#Text= contain very little water, such as the pulses and cereals when cooked
#Text= absorb a very large quantity; this is particularly the case in making
#Text= porridge.
#Text=Cabbage, cauliflower, Spanish onions and turnips, after cooking
#Text= contain even 97 per cent. of water.
#Text=Roast beef contains on an average 48
#Text= per cent., and cooked round steak with fat removed 63 per cent. of water.
#Text=It is customary at meal times to drink water, tea, coffee, beer, wine, &c.
#Text=When a meal contains any considerable quantity of fresh fruits there need
#Text= be no desire to drink.
#Text=Notwithstanding that fruits contain so much water,
#Text= a dietary consisting of fruits with nuts, to which may be added bread and
#Text= vegetables, will contain less water than the total quantity usually
#Text= consumed by a person taking the more customary highly cooked and seasoned
#Text= foods.
#Text=An advantage is that the water in fruits is in a wholesome
#Text= condition, free from the pollution often met with in the water used for
#Text= drinking purposes.
#Text=Raw fruits favour mastication, with its consequent
#Text= advantages, whilst cooked and soft food discourages it.
#Text=Plums and what are
#Text= termed stone fruits, if eaten in more than very small quantities, are apt
#Text= to disagree.
#Text=Persons with good digestions can take fruit with bread,
#Text= biscuits and with uncooked foods without any inconvenience.
#Text=Fruit is more

#Text=There
#Text= are many persons who cannot eat of some particular food, although it may
#Text= be quite wholesome to others.
#Text=Sometimes it is a psychological rather than
#Text= a physiological disability, which may he overcome by an effort of the
#Text= will.
#Text=At other times it seems to have no connection with the imagination,
#Text= although it is not always possible to give a sound reason for it.
#Text=In the
#Text= main, of course, there are principles of dietetics applicable to all
#Text= alike, but in regard to details, everyone should make rules for himself,
#Text= according to his experience.
#Text=When there appears no real reason for an
#Text= idiosyncrasy, a little humouring of our taste and digestion will often
#Text= overcome it, to our advantage.
#Text=It is generally those of delicate
#Text= constitution who are most sensitive.
#Text=Some cannot eat oatmeal except in
#Text= small quantity.
#Text=Olive and other vegetable oils, even when of good quality
#Text= cannot be taken by many people, whilst others find them quite as
#Text= wholesome, or even better than butter.
#Text=Vegetarians can generally detect
#Text= lard in pastry both by its taste and its after effects, although those
#Text= accustomed to this fat do not object to it.
#Text=It is also surprising how some
#Text= individual  '  s tastes and habits will vary at different periods of their
#Text= lives.
#Text=One form of dyspepsia is due to undigested starch remaining in the stomach
#Text= and causing an excessive secretion of hydrochloric acid.
#Text=As long as
#Text= proteid food is present, the pepsin and acid expend themselves on it, and
#Text= are removed together.
#Text=The undigested starch continues to stimulate gastric
#Text= secretion, and the acid residuum causes pain, heartburn and flatulence.
#Text=If
#Text= there be also any butyric acid, or some other fatty acid, derived from
#Text= milk, butter, cheese, &c., there will be acid eructations.
#Text=For this form
#Text= of indigestion there are several methods of treatment.
#Text=First; the very
#Text= thorough cooking of all starchy food, and it is an advantage to take a
#Text= little good extract of malt, either at the time of eating or directly
#Text= afterwards.
#Text=The diastase of the malt has the same action on starch as the
#Text= ptyalin in the saliva.
#Text=It is better, scientifically, to have the
#Text= farinaceous food at about 130° F.
#Text=(as hot as the mouth can bear will do),
#Text= and then to add malt extract.
#Text=On keeping the mixture warm, from a few
#Text= minutes to half an hour or more, the starch is digested and rendered
#Text= soluble.
#Text=Such food is not very pleasant to take.
#Text=The food known as Grape
#Text= Nuts has been treated in a similar manner.
#Text=The use of malt extract,
#Text= however, seems a clumsy substitute for salivary digestion.
#Text=Second; the
#Text= eating of starch in the form of hard and dry biscuits, crusts and other
#Text= hard food, which demand thorough mastication and insalivation, and the
#Text=keeping in the mouth for a long while, during which the saliva has time to
#Text= act.
#Text=This is the best plan.
#Text=Third; the taking of sodium bicarbonate
#Text= towards the end of the period of digestion, in order to neutralise the
#Text= acid in the stomach.
#Text=This gives relief, but does not cure, as the dose has
#Text= to be repeated after each meal; in course of time the quantity of soda has
#Text= sometimes to be increased to an alarming extent.
#Text=Fourth; the abstention
#Text= from starchy foods and the substitution of an exclusive flesh dietary.
#Text=In
#Text= the "Salisbury" treatment, raw minced beef is given.
#Text=This method often
#Text= gives immediate relief, but its ultimate effect on the kidneys and other
#Text= organs is very bad.
#Text=No hard and fast rule can be laid down as to the number of meals into
#Text= which the daily amount of food required should be divided.
#Text=The stomach
#Text= appears to work to the best advantage when it is full, or nearly so, and
#Text= the appetite is appeased.
#Text=Three approximately equal meals seems to be a
#Text= convenient division.
#Text=Dr.
#Text=Dewey and his followers advise only two meals a
#Text= day, and it seems incontestable that many persons find the plan
#Text= advantageous.
#Text=These are generally adults with weak digestions, or elderly
#Text= persons who, on account of their age and the sluggish action of their
#Text= assimilative functions, require comparatively little food.
#Text=Children, on
#Text=comparatively insipid character of the food and want of appetite.
#Text=In
#Text= making a change to a vegetarian diet, such foods had better be taken that
#Text= are rather rich in proteid, and that approximate somewhat in their flavour
#Text= and manner of cooking to that used previously.
#Text=A further change to a
#Text= simpler diet can afterwards gradually be made, according to conviction,
#Text= tastes and bodily adaptability.
#Text=It must not be expected that a change,
#Text= even an ultimately very advantageous one, will always meet with an
#Text= immediate and proper response from digestive and assimilative organs which
#Text= have been accustomed for many years, perhaps by inheritance for
#Text= generations, to another manner of living.
#Text=There are several preparations
#Text= produced from centrifugalised milk--that is milk from which the butter fat
#Text= has been removed, which consist chiefly of proteid.
#Text=These have a value in
#Text= increasing the proteid contents of foods which may be thought deficient.
#Text=The addition of these manufactured products appear unnecessary, as most
#Text= of our food contains an abundance of proteid, and we can easily limit the
#Text= quantity or avoid altogether those that are thought defective.
#Text=The later apologists for a flesh diet have had to admit that it is not a
#Text= physiological necessity; but they have attempted to justify its use by a
#Text= theory somewhat as follows.
#Text=It is admitted, that any excess of proteid

#Text= such high livers are usually common-place, intellectually, and of
#Text= deteriorated physique.
#Text=The aristocracy who are generally high livers,
#Text= notwithstanding their great advantages of education, travel and leisure,

#Text=In the recent war
#Text= the frugal living Japanese soldier has proved himself the most enduring

#Text=What is called high-feeding, is of the greatest

#Text=Food Adjuncts and Drugs.
#Text=--In addition to the nutrients and the small
#Text= quantity of indigestible fibre of which we have already written, food
#Text= generally contains small quantities of substances which are difficult to
#Text= classify, and whose action on the body is but imperfectly understood.
#Text=Many
#Text= of these possess pungent or strong odours and flavours.
#Text=To them, various
#Text= fruits, meats, etc., owe much of their characteristic differences of
#Text= taste.
#Text=When pure the proteids and starches are devoid of taste.
#Text=Such oils
#Text= and fats as are generally eaten have also but little flavour, providing
#Text=they are free from rancidity and of good quality.
#Text=The sugars differ from
#Text= the other nutrients in possessing a more or less decided taste.
#Text=The free
#Text= vegetable acids also strongly affect the sense of taste, but they are only
#Text= consumed in small quantities.
#Text=A drug may be defined as a substance which modifies the functions of the
#Text= body or of some organ without sensibly imparting nourishment.
#Text=This action
#Text= may be one of stimulation or of depression.
#Text=A drug is taken for its
#Text= medicinal action, a food adjunct for its modifying action on food.
#Text=It is
#Text= impossible to give a quite satisfactory definition, or to draw sharp
#Text= distinctions.
#Text=For example, tea, coffee, alcohol and tobacco are sometimes
#Text= placed in one group, and sometimes in another, according to opinion of
#Text= their action and the definition of the terms food adjuncts, drugs and
#Text= poisons.
#Text=The difference of grouping often depends upon intensity rather
#Text= than of kind of action.
#Text=If taken frequently and not in quantity sufficient
#Text= to have a markedly medicinal action, such things are generally called food
#Text= adjuncts or supplementary foods, although much may be said in favour of a
#Text= different view.
#Text=The volatile oils of mustard, caraway, cloves, etc., are
#Text= used in medicine; also the alkaloids of coffee and cocoa.
#Text=Even honey is
#Text= used as a mild laxative for infants; that is, as a drug.
#Text=The difference
#Text=cereals, wheat, oatmeal, etc., and fruit.
#Text=On the other hand there are
#Text= races who enjoy stronger flavoured food, including such things as garlic,
#Text= curry, pickles, pepper, strong cheese, meat extracts, rancid fats, dried
#Text= and smoked fish, high game or still more decomposed flesh, offal and
#Text= various disgusting things.
#Text=The Greenlanders will eat with the keenest
#Text= appetite, the half-frozen, half-putrid head and fins of the seal, after
#Text= it has been preserved under the grass of summer.
#Text=In Burmah and Sumatra a
#Text= mess is made by pounding together prawns, shrimps, or any cheap fish; this
#Text= is frequently allowed to become partially putrid.
#Text=It is largely used as a
#Text= condiment for mixing with their rice.
#Text=Numerous examples of this sort could
#Text= be given.
#Text=There is scarcely anything that it is possible to eat, but has
#Text= been consumed with relish by some tribe or other.
#Text=The strongest flavoured,
#Text= and to our minds most disgusting foods are eaten by the least intelligent
#Text= and most brutal races.
#Text=It is hunger that compels the poor African bushman
#Text= to eat anything he can get, and the Hottentot not only the flesh, but the
#Text= entrails of cattle which die naturally, and this last he has come to think
#Text= exquisite when boiled in beast-blood.
#Text=All this shows a wonderful range of
#Text= adaptability in the human body, but it would not be right to say that all
#Text= such food is equally wholesome.
#Text=The most advanced and civilised races,
#Text= especially the more delicately organised of them are the most fastidious,
#Text=whilst it is the most brutal, that take the most rank and strongly
#Text= flavoured foods.
#Text=Even amongst the civilised there are great differences.
#Text=The assimilative and nervous systems can be trained to tolerate injurious
#Text= influences to a remarkable degree.
#Text=A striking example is seen in the
#Text= nausea commonly produced by the first pipe of tobacco, and the way the
#Text= body may in time be persuaded, not only to tolerate many times such a
#Text= quantity without manifesting any unpleasant feelings, but to receive
#Text= pleasure from the drug.
#Text=Opium or laudanum may be taken in gradually
#Text= increasing quantities, until such a dose is taken as would at first have
#Text= produced death, yet now without causing any immediate or very apparent
#Text= harm.
#Text=Nearly all drugs loose much of their first effect on continued use.
#Text=Not only is this so, but a sudden discontinuance of a drug may cause
#Text= distress, as the body, when free from the artificial stimulation to which
#Text= it has become habituated, falls into a sluggish or torpid condition.
#Text=For
#Text= the enjoyment of food two things are equally necessary, a healthy and keen
#Text= appetite and suitable food; without the first no food, however good and
#Text= skilfully prepared, will give satisfaction.
#Text=The sense of taste resides in
#Text= certain of the papilloe of the tongue, and to a much less degree in the
#Text= palate.
#Text=Tastes may be classified into sweet, bitter, acid and saline.
#Text=Sweet tastes are best appreciated by the tip, acid by the side, and bitter
#Text=by the back of the tongue.
#Text=Hot or pungent substances produce sensations of
#Text= general feeling, which obscure any strictly gustatory sensations which may
#Text= be present at the same time.
#Text=To affect the taste the food must enter into
#Text= solution.
#Text=Like the other senses, taste may be rendered more delicate by
#Text= cultivation.
#Text=Flavours are really odours, and the word smell would be more
#Text= appropriate.
#Text=For example, what we call the taste of an onion, the flavour
#Text= of fruit, etc.
#Text=(independent of the sweetness or sourness of the fruit) is
#Text= due to the nose.
#Text=Much has been written on the necessity of making food tasty, so as to
#Text= stimulate the appetite and digestion.
#Text=It is urged that unless this is done
#Text= food will not be eaten in sufficient quantity.
#Text=Innumerable receipts (some
#Text= very elaborate) have been published for this purpose.
#Text=All this is supposed
#Text= to increase the enjoyment of food.
#Text=The Anglo-Saxon race--the race whose
#Text= dietary is the most elaborate--is especially subject to digestive
#Text= derangements, and without good digestion and the consequent healthy
#Text= appetite, no food will give full gustatory pleasure.
#Text=The most wholesome
#Text= food, and that which can be eaten most frequently without weariness, is
#Text= mildly flavoured and simply prepared.
#Text=Plain bread is an example; whereas
#Text= sweet bread, currant bread, etc., though agreeable in small quantity, or
#Text=as an occasional delicacy, soon palls on the appetite.
#Text=Rice is the poorest
#Text= and mildest flavoured of the cereals, it is therefore often, perhaps
#Text= generally, made more tasty by the addition of fish, curry, etc.
#Text=The bulk
#Text= of the Chinese live on rice, with the exception of only 3 or 4 ounces of
#Text= fish per day, and they are a fine, big and strong race.
#Text=The Japanese
#Text= labourer lives on similar food.
#Text=In India rice is the food most in use,
#Text= though many other cereals are eaten there.
#Text=Other races live chiefly on
#Text= fruits.
#Text=It appears that the digestive organs will perform their functions
#Text= perfectly with the mildest flavoured food.
#Text=There is nothing surprising in
#Text= this.
#Text=The strongest, most intelligent, and largest animals are those which
#Text= feed on grass, herbs and fruits.
#Text=Even the African lion is no match for the
#Text= gorilla.
#Text=The lion and tiger are capable of great strength, but they cannot
#Text= put it forth for long periods as can the herbivora.
#Text=Our most useful
#Text= animal, the horse, can exert much more muscular energy, weight for weight,
#Text= than any of the carnivora.
#Text=The cost of feeding one of the herbivora is
#Text= much less than that of one of the carnivora of the same weight.
#Text=This is so
#Text= whether we take the cost of purchasing the food; or the expenditure of
#Text= time, labour and energy on the part of man or of natural forces in the
#Text= production of the food.
#Text=Herbs, roots, corn and fruit are produced much
#Text= more abundantly and freely than the corresponding quantity of sheep, deer,
#Text=etc., on which the carnivora feed.
#Text=The restlessness, craving for novelty, and love of excitement, so
#Text= characteristic of the Anglo-Saxon, and to a less extent of some other
#Text= European races, has its correspondence in the food of these races.
#Text=Highly-seasoned and nitrogenous foods act as a stimulant and favour
#Text= spasmodic, and for a time perhaps, great intellectual and physical
#Text= exertion, with a succeeding period of exhaustion.
#Text=Simpler food favours
#Text= long, sustained, uniform muscular strength, clearness of intellect, and
#Text= contentment.
#Text=Let no one misunderstand us; we do not assert that all who
#Text= live on simple food have either clear intellects or are contented, because
#Text= there are other factors besides food, but that such qualities are more
#Text= easily retained or obtained under that condition.
#Text=It is well known that
#Text= the over-fed and badly fed are the most irritable and discontented Those
#Text= living on a stimulating dietary consisting largely of flesh have their
#Text= chief successes in feats of short duration.
#Text=Simple and abstemious living
#Text= individuals or races excel in laborious work requiring endurance over long
#Text= periods, such as long walking, cycling, and other athletic feats and long
#Text= military campaigns.
#Text=left, the same kind is not equally suitable to everyone, nor even to the
#Text= same person at different periods.
#Text=A delicately balanced, fine-grained, high-toned mind and body responds to
#Text= every tender influence, and is painfully jarred by that which is coarse.
#Text=To such, fruits and delicately flavoured and easily digested foods are
#Text= doubtless best and conducive to purity and clearness of thought.
#Text=A
#Text= coarse-grained, badly poised, roughly working body and spirit, is
#Text= non-responsive except to loud or coarse impulses; and such a one  '  s
#Text= appetite is gratified, not by simple but by coarsely seasoned foods.
#Text=A person who is accustomed to a stimulating dietary of flesh-foods,
#Text= especially if well-seasoned, finds a simple diet unsatisfying.
#Text=Should such
#Text= persons dine off simple vegetarian food, there is a tendency to
#Text= over-eating.
#Text=The less stimulating food fails to rouse the digestive organs
#Text= and to appease the appetite; although an ample supply of nourishment be
#Text= consumed.
#Text=This is the reason why so many imagine that it is necessary to
#Text= eat a larger quantity of food if it be vegetable.
#Text=Should a distressing
#Text= fulness and flatulence result from their over-feeding, they lay the blame
#Text= to the vegetarian dietary instead of to themselves.
#Text=Most persons, on
#Text=changing to a vegetarian dietary, commence by imitating flesh dishes in
#Text= appearance and flavour and even in the names.
#Text=There is the additional
#Text= inducement that the food may be attractive and palatable to friends who
#Text= lack sympathy with the aesthetic and humane principles of the diet.
#Text=After
#Text= a while many of them incline to simpler flavoured foods.
#Text=They revert to
#Text= the unperverted taste of childhood, for children love sweets, fruits, and
#Text= mild-flavoured foods rather than savouries.
#Text=One who loves savouries, as a
#Text= rule, cares much less for fruits.
#Text=By compounding and cooking, a very great
#Text= variety of foods can be prepared, but the differences in taste are much
#Text= less than is usually, supposed.
#Text=The effect of seasoning instead of
#Text= increasing the range, diminishes it, by dulling the finer perception of
#Text= flavours.
#Text=The predominating seasoning also obscures everything else.
#Text=The
#Text= mixture of foods produces a conglomeration of tastes in which any
#Text= particular or distinct flavours are obscured, resulting in a general
#Text= sameness.
#Text=It is often stated that as an ordinary flesh-eater has the
#Text= choice of a greater range of foods and flavours than a vegetarian, he can
#Text= obtain more enjoyment, and that the latter is disagreeably restricted.
#Text=Certainly he has the choice, but does he avail himself of it to any
#Text= considerable extent?
#Text=No one cares to take all the different kinds of food,
#Text= whether of animal or vegetable that are possible.
#Text=Of edible animals but a
#Text=very few kinds are eaten.
#Text=A person who particularly relishes and partakes
#Text= largely of flesh-foods will reject as insipid and unsatisfying many
#Text= mild-flavoured foods at one end of the scale.
#Text=The vegetarian may abstain
#Text= from foods at the opposite end of the scale, not always from humane
#Text= reasons, but because they are unpleasant.
#Text=Thus there may be little to
#Text= choose between the mere range of flavours that give enjoyment to each
#Text= class of persons.
#Text=The sense of taste is in its character and range lower
#Text= than the sense of sight and hearing.
#Text=The cultivation of the taste for
#Text= savouries seems to blunt the taste for fruits and the delicate foods.
#Text=The
#Text= grass and herbs on which the herbivora subsist, seems to our imagination
#Text= of little flavour and monotonous; but they eat with every sign of
#Text= enjoyment, deliberately munching their food as though to get its full
#Text= flavour.
#Text=In all probability they find a considerable range of flavours in
#Text= the great varieties of grasses commonly found together in a pasture.
#Text=Our elaborate cooking customs entail a vast amount of labour.
#Text=They
#Text= necessitate the cost, trouble and dirt from having fires in great excess
#Text= of that required for warmth: the extra time in preparing, mixing and
#Text= attending to food which has to be cooked: and the large number of greasy
#Text= and soiled utensils which have to be cleaned.
#Text=Cooked savoury food is
#Text=generally much nicer eaten hot, and this necessitates fires and attention
#Text= just previous to the meal.
#Text=We have already said that soft cooked food
#Text= discourages mastication and leads to defective teeth.
#Text=Our elaborate
#Text= cookery is mainly due to our custom of eating so largely of flesh, whilst
#Text= the eating of flesh would receive a great impetus on the discovery of the
#Text= art of cooking.
#Text=Flesh can only be eaten with relish and with safety when
#Text= cooked.
#Text=Such a large proportion of it is infected with parasites, or is
#Text= otherwise diseased, that it would he dangerous to eat it raw, even were it
#Text= palatable in such a state.
#Text=In those countries where man eats flesh in a
#Text= raw or semi-cooked form, parasitic diseases are common.
#Text=There is not the
#Text= least doubt that our habit of eating so much cooked food is responsible
#Text= for much over-eating, hasty eating, dyspepsia and illness.
#Text=In regard to
#Text= the making of bread, porridge, and many other comparatively simple
#Text= prepared foods, the advantages of cooking seem overwhelmingly great.
#Text=With
#Text= our present imperfect knowledge and conflicting opinions, it is
#Text= impossible to arrive at any satisfactory conclusion, and the whole
#Text= question requires careful and impartial investigation.
#Text=Experiments have
#Text= been made with animals, chiefly pigs, with cooked and uncooked clover,
#Text= hay, corn, meal, etc.
#Text=(U.S.
#Text=Department of Agriculture).
#Text=It was found that
#Text= the food was more or less diminished in digestibility by cooking.
#Text=At least
#Text=13 separate series of experiments with pigs in different part of the
#Text= country have been reported.
#Text=In 10 of these trials there has been a
#Text= positive loss from cooking the food.
#Text=The amount of food required to
#Text= produce in the animal a pound gain in weight was larger when the food had
#Text= been cooked than when it was given raw.
#Text=In some cases, the increased
#Text= quantity of food required after cooking was considerable.
#Text=Those who live on uncooked food contend that a smaller quantity of
#Text= nourishment is required.
#Text=As uncooked food requires more mastication and is
#Text= eaten more slowly, there is a better flow of saliva and time is given for
#Text= the digestive organs to be gradually brought into complete action, and
#Text= finally for the appeasing of the appetite.
#Text=In the case of the members of
#Text= the fruitarian family, whose food was uncooked, and of whom we have
#Text= previously written, the quantity of nutriment taken was much less than
#Text= that thought necessary, even after making full allowance for their small
#Text= stature and weight.
